section.heading: 7.1 Diagonalization of Symmetric Matrices
section.paragraph: A symmetric matrix is a matrix $$A$$ such that $$A^{T} = A$$ . Such a matrix is necessarily square. Its main diagonal entries are arbitrary, but its other entries occur in pairs—on opposite sides of the main diagonal.

section.paragraph: Theorem 1﻿ explains why the eigenvectors in Example 2﻿ are orthogonal—they correspond to distinct eigenvalues.

note.title: Theorem 1
note.heading: Theorem 1
note.paragraph: If $$A$$ is symmetric, then any two eigenvectors from different eigenspaces are orthogonal.

section.heading: Proof
section.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{v}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{v}_{2}$$ be eigenvectors that correspond to distinct eigenvalues, say, $$\text{λ} _{1}$$ and $$\text{λ} _{2}$$ . To show that $$\textbf{v}_{1} \cdot \textbf{v}_{2} = 0$$ , compute

$$\lambda_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} \cdot \textbf{v}_{2} & = (\lambda_{1} \textbf{v}_{1} )^{T} \textbf{v}_{2} = \left(( A \textbf{v}_{1} )\right)^{T} \textbf{v}_{2} & & \text{Since} \textbf{v}_{1 } \text{is} \text{an} \text{eigenvector} & = ( \textbf{v}_{1}^{T} A^{T} ) \textbf{v}_{2} = \textbf{v}_{1}^{T} ( A \textbf{v}_{2} ) & & \text{Since} A^{T} = A & = \textbf{v}_{1}^{T} (\lambda_{2} \textbf{v}_{2} ) & & \text{Since} \textbf{v}_{2} \text{is} \text{an} \text{eigenvector} & = \lambda_{2} \textbf{v}_{1}^{T} \textbf{v}_{2} = \lambda_{2} \textbf{v}_{1} \cdot \textbf{v}_{2} & &$$
Hence $$( \text{λ} _{1} - \text{λ} _{2})\textbf{v}_{1} \cdot \textbf{v}_{2} = 0$$ . But $$\text{λ} _{1} - \text{λ} _{2} \neq 0$$ , so $$\textbf{v}_{1} \cdot \textbf{v}_{2} = 0$$ .

The special type of diagonalization in Example 2 is crucial for the theory of symmetric matrices. An $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is said to be orthogonally diagonalizable if there are an orthogonal matrix $$P$$ (with $$P^{- 1} = P^{T}$$ ) and a diagonal matrix $$D$$ such that
$$A = \left(P D P\right)^{T} = \left(P D P\right)^{- 1}$$
Such a diagonalization requires $$n$$ linearly independent and orthonormal eigenvectors. When is this possible? If $$A$$ is orthogonally diagonalizable as in (1), then
$$A^{T} = \left(\right. \left(P D P\right)^{T} \left.\right)^{T} = P^{T T} D^{T} P^{T} = \left(P D P\right)^{T} = A$$

Thus $$A$$ is symmetric! Theorem 2 below shows that, conversely, every symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable. The proof is much harder and is omitted; the main idea for a proof will be given after Theorem 3.

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
note.paragraph: An $$n \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if $$A$$ is a symmetric matrix.

section.paragraph: This theorem is rather amazing, because the work in Chapter 5 would suggest that it is usually impossible to tell when a matrix is diagonalizable. But this is not the case for symmetric matrices.
The next example treats a matrix whose eigenvalues are not all distinct.

section.heading: The Spectral Theorem
section.paragraph: The set of eigenvalues of a matrix $$A$$ is sometimes called the spectrum of $$A$$ , and the following description of the eigenvalues is called a spectral theorem.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
The Spectral Theorem for Symmetric Matrices
note.paragraph: An $$n \times n$$ symmetric matrix $$A$$ has the following properties:

list.item: The dimension of the eigenspace for each eigenvalue $$\text{λ}$$ equals the multiplicity of $$\text{λ}$$ as a root of the characteristic equation.
The eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal, in the sense that eigenvectors corresponding to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

section.heading: Spectral Decomposition
section.paragraph: Suppose $$A = {PDP}^{- 1}$$ , where the columns of $$P$$ are orthonormal eigenvectors $$\mathbf{u}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{u}_{n}$$ of $$A$$ and the corresponding eigenvalues $$\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{2}$$ are in the diagonal matrix $$D$$ . Then, since $$P^{- 1} = P^{T}$$ ,

$$A & = & P D P^{T} = [ \textbf{u}_{1} \hdots \textbf{u}_{n} ] \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\lambda_{1} & & 0 \\ & \ddots & \\ 0 & & \lambda_{n}\end{matrix} \left]\right. \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{u}_{1}^{T} \\ \vdots \\ \textbf{u}_{n}^{T}\end{matrix} \left]\right. & = & [\lambda_{1} \textbf{u}_{1} \hdots \lambda_{n} \textbf{u}_{n} ] \left[\right. \begin{matrix}\textbf{u}_{1}^{T} \\ \vdots \\ \textbf{u}_{n}^{T}\end{matrix} \left]\right.$$
Using the column–row expansion of a product (Theorem 10 in Section 2.4), we can write

This representation of $$A$$ is called a spectral decomposition of $$A$$ because it breaks up $$A$$ into pieces determined by the spectrum (eigenvalues) of $$A$$ . Each term in (2) is an $$n \times n$$ matrix of rank $$1$$ . For example, every column of $$\text{λ} _{1}\textbf{u}_{1}\textbf{u}_{1}^{T}$$ is a multiple of $$\textbf{u}_{1}$$ . Furthermore, each matrix $$\textbf{u}_{j}\textbf{u}_{j}^{T}$$ is a projection matrix in the sense that for each $$\textbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the vector $$(\textbf{u}_{j}\textbf{u}_{j}^{T})\textbf{x}$$ is the orthogonal projection of $$\textbf{x}$$ onto the subspace spanned by $$\textbf{u}_{j}$$ . (See Exercise 41.)

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: When $$A$$ is symmetric and not too large, modern high-performance computer algorithms calculate eigenvalues and eigenvectors with great precision. They apply a sequence of similarity transformations to $$A$$ involving orthogonal matrices. The diagonal entries of the transformed matrices converge rapidly to the eigenvalues of $$A$$ . (See the Numerical Notes in Section 5.2.) Using orthogonal matrices generally prevents numerical errors from accumulating during the process. When $$A$$ is symmetric, the sequence of orthogonal matrices combines to form an orthogonal matrix whose columns are eigenvectors of $$A$$ .

A nonsymmetric matrix cannot have a full set of orthogonal eigenvectors, but the algorithm still produces fairly accurate eigenvalues. After that, nonorthogonal techniques are needed to calculate eigenvectors.
